title: Path Channels and Plan Extension Kernels
one_liner: A trained game-playing network hides its plans as specific patterns in its memory, and extends them using learned rules that work like a two-way push from boxes and goals.
lead: When you teach a neural network to play Sokoban (a box-pushing puzzle game) using reinforcement learning, it learns to plan which moves to make. But where does it store that plan inside its brain? This paper reverse-engineers the network's actual memory to find that plans live in specific channels (think of them as filing cabinets), and the network expands those plans using learned rules that work like propagating waves outward from goals and boxes—then bouncing back when they hit a wall.

problem.h2: Neural networks learn in the dark
paras: When you train a network to play a puzzle game using reinforcement learning (a trial-and-error method where you reward good moves and punish bad ones), the network learns to win. But we have almost no idea how it does it. The network keeps its strategy locked inside billions of numbers called weights and activations (the intermediate calculations it makes while thinking). A beginner might hope the network stores an explicit plan—like a checklist of moves—but that seems too organized for something trained randomly. More likely, the network hides its planning scattered across thousands of interconnected pieces. Understanding the real mechanism would let us trust, predict, and maybe control what the network does.

The naive approach: look at the network's weights and activations and try to describe them. Weights are numbers that define how information flows between layers; activations are the numbers the network computes at each step. But there are so many of them that this is like reading a phone book—true but useless. We need to find the hidden structure: which parts do the planning, and how do they actually work?

callout.html: The paper found that plans are stored as activations in specific channels, and the network extends them using learned rules (shifting and combining nearby values) that work like a two-way wave.

steps.text: Convert raw image of the Sokoban board into a lower-level representation.
Memory layers process the encoded board and previous memory, producing activations in specific channels.
Learned shifting-and-combining rules expand activations from box positions forward and from goal positions backward.
Negative values at walls cause the wave to bounce and cancel, pruning explored paths as the network backtracks through plans.
Final layer combines all plan channels to choose the next move.

paras: The paper changes how we look at a trained network. Instead of reading all its weights and activations as a black box, it identifies specific channels (slices of memory) that carry plan information, and interprets them as a structured planning algorithm.

hidden.h2: The path channel activation: where plans hide
hidden.name: channel activation for a given location and direction
paras: A path channel is a specific slice of the network's hidden state (memory). At each location on the board, each channel stores a number (an activation) that represents whether that location in that direction is part of the plan. A high activation means: when a box sits here, push it in this direction.

The paper measures this by ablating (removing) one channel at a time and checking how much the network's planning accuracy drops. If removing channel 5 makes the network forget how to push boxes left, then channel 5 is the left-push-path channel.

heat.caption: High activation (dark) at a location means the plan includes that move there.

reads.html: A channel is like a slot in memory that marks which moves to make at which spots. When the slot is full (high activation), the move is part of the plan.
Path channels encode future plans as positional activations across the hidden state of the ConvLSTM layers, detectable via single-step cache ablation.

paras: The network starts with an observation (the board state). It passes this through an encoder (a simple layer that looks at nearby pixels and combines them, with no activation function, so it is just linear math). Then the network runs three memory layers three times in a row—nine passes total per decision.

During these passes, the network constructs the plan in two directions at once. Starting from the locations of the boxes, it propagates forward activation in path channels (this says: from the box, we can push in direction X). Separately, starting from the goal location, it propagates backward activation (this says: the goal is reached via direction Y). These waves travel through convolutional kernels—learned rules that copy and shift the activation one square at a time.

When either wave hits an obstacle (a wall or immovable block), the network places a negative value there. This negative value acts like a stop sign. The kernel rules use the negative value to propagate backward, which cancels the forward wave—this is backtracking. It lets the network explore alternative plans. After nine passes, all plans are explored and pruned. The final MLP head reads the remaining positive activations in all channels and decides which move to make.

stages.s: Encoder: turn image into low-level patterns
Run 9 ConvLSTM passes: extend plans from boxes forward and from goal backward
Obstacles create negative values, which backtrack and cancel bad paths

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose the box is at position (3, 5) and the right-channel activation is 0.8 at that spot.
The right kernel shifts this 0.8 one square right to position (3, 6). The kernel is learned to preserve magnitudes, so activation at (3, 6) becomes 0.8.
If there is a wall at (3, 7), we place obs_neg = -1 there. The kernel tries to shift the 0.8 to (3, 7) but the negative value cancels it: 0.8 + (−1) = −0.2.
The negative activation propagates backward left, canceling activations at (3, 6) and (3, 5). The backtracking is complete; this direction is pruned.

math.note: The kernel is just multiplication and addition (convolution), so activations propagate and cancel without any learned switching logic.

items.html: In a different network or training regime, path channels might overlap or encode multiple concepts, making the channel interpretation fragile.
If many obstacles create long chains of negative values, the cancellation waves might not converge cleanly within the nine passes, leaving the plan ambiguous.
The learned rules are fixed-size, so a network trained on small boards (say twenty by twenty squares) may fail on larger boards (thirty by thirty squares) where plans are longer.
When channels are well-separated and obstacles are moderate, the mechanism is transparent and lets you predict or even edit the plan by hand.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a minimal Sokoban solver that stores plans explicitly: one channel per direction. At each step, propagate activations from the box in all four directions, marking which squares can be reached. When you hit an obstacle, mark it negative and backtrack. After a fixed number of iterations, read off the activation values and pick the direction with the highest activation at the box location. Compare this naive explicit planner to a trained ConvLSTM network. You should see that the trained network is doing mechanically similar operations—just learned and embedded inside its weights.
demo.closing: The demo must show that the explicit plan mechanism and the trained network produce the same moves on new puzzles, proving the interpretation is real.
